questions.question: What goes into a high-quality blameless postmortem?
questions.title: Blameless Postmortem: Template, Process, Culture
questions.direct_answer: A blameless postmortem has six sections: **Summary** (what happened, when, impact), **Timeline** (minute-by-minute with UTC timestamps), **Root cause** (contributing factors, not 'human error'), **Resolution** (how it was fixed), **What went well / poorly** (both sides), and **Action items** (specific owners, due dates, linked tickets). Blameless means focusing on *systems* that allowed the mistake, not the individual who made it. Publish within 5 business days; review in a group; track action items to completion. The purpose is learning, not punishment.

interviewer_intent.testing: Engineering maturity, culture understanding, and SRE practice
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing blame-heavy postmortems; listing action items without owners/dates; not publishing publicly; skipping the 'what went well' section
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss psychological safety, the 5-whys vs systems thinking, action item tracking to completion, and the cost of postmortems that stay private

sections.title: Postmortems Are the Receipt You Get for Paying with an Outage
sections.content:
Every production incident costs the company: users affected, engineering time, revenue lost, trust dented. The postmortem is what the company receives in return — a written artifact that turns a painful incident into organizational learning.

A good postmortem is **blameless**: it focuses on the systems, processes, and context that allowed the mistake, not on the individual who made it. An engineer who typed the wrong command was able to type it because:
- The command wasn't behind sufficient safeguards
- The UI/CLI didn't warn them
- The on-call process didn't require review for destructive operations
- Training didn't cover this failure mode

Fixing 'the engineer' doesn't prevent recurrence; fixing 'the system' does.

The standard structure, used by Google, Etsy, GitHub, Netflix, and hundreds of mature orgs:

1. **Summary** — TL;DR of what happened, duration, impact (users affected, revenue)
2. **Timeline** — every notable event, in UTC, minute-level granularity
3. **Root cause & contributing factors** — multi-factor analysis, not 'human error'
4. **Resolution** — how it was mitigated and fixed
5. **What went well / what went poorly** — both sides, honestly
6. **Action items** — specific, owned, with due dates and tickets

Published within 5 business days; reviewed in a group meeting; action items tracked to completion. The meeting is the learning event; the document is the artifact.

Without this structure, outages repeat. With it, organizations get better over time.

sections.title: Template Section by Section
sections.content:
**Summary**

```
Service: payment-service
Incident date: 2026-04-22 14:00 UTC
Duration: 32 minutes
Severity: SEV-1
Impact: 15% of checkout requests failed; estimated $120K revenue loss
Root cause category: Deployment
Authors: @jane-oncall, @bob-sre
```

**Timeline (UTC, specific)**

```
14:00 — Deploy of payment-service v2.4.1 starts (normal canary)
14:02 — Canary pod at 100%; no alarms yet
14:07 — PagerDuty fires: payment_5xx_rate > 1% for 5 minutes
14:09 — On-call @jane acknowledges; opens incident channel
14:12 — Identifies recent deploy as correlation via deploy dashboard
14:14 — Attempts to roll back via Argo; rollback fails due to stuck sync
14:18 — Manually scales payment-service-v2.4.0 deployment to desiredCount
14:22 — Traffic stabilizes; error rate back to baseline
14:32 — Incident closed
```

Use specific times, not vague phrases. 'About 10 minutes in' is useless. '14:14 UTC' is analyzable.

**Root cause and contributing factors**

Not: 'Jane pushed a bug to production'.

Yes: '(1) v2.4.1 contained a Hibernate query that generated N+1 under load; (2) load tests used 10 RPS, production sees 500 RPS, so N+1 was invisible in CI; (3) canary deploy at 100% exposed all traffic simultaneously rather than ramping; (4) auto-rollback wasn't configured; (5) manual rollback via Argo was blocked by an unrelated stuck sync.'

Multiple contributing factors; each becomes a potential action item.

**Resolution**

Short-term: manually scaled previous version, redirected traffic. Long-term: query fix deployed in v2.4.2 with performance test reproducing the N+1.

**What went well / what went poorly**

*Went well:*
- Alert fired within 5 minutes of degradation
- On-call acknowledged within 2 minutes
- Runbook existed and pointed to the right dashboards
- Team coordination via incident channel was smooth

*Went poorly:*
- Canary strategy deployed 100% too fast (no ramp)
- Auto-rollback not configured
- Manual rollback path blocked by unrelated Argo stuck sync
- Load tests not representative of production traffic

Both sides matter. Celebrating what worked reinforces good behavior; examining what didn't reveals systemic gaps.

**Action items (SMART)**

| Item | Owner | Due | Ticket |
|---|---|---|---|
| Configure auto-rollback on payment-service | @sre-team | 2026-04-29 | PAY-1234 |
| Add N+1 detection to CI via p6spy assertions | @backend-team | 2026-05-13 | PAY-1235 |
| Increase load-test traffic to match prod (500 RPS) | @qa-team | 2026-05-06 | QA-987 |
| Fix Argo stuck sync recovery path | @platform-team | 2026-04-26 | PLAT-555 |
| Run quarterly rollback drill | @sre-team | 2026-05-30 | SRE-200 |

Every action item has: specific outcome, single owner, due date, linked ticket. Vague items like 'improve monitoring' are death — nothing happens.

sections.title: The Culture That Makes Postmortems Work
sections.content:
**Blameless means blameless, not responsibility-free.** Engineers still own their work; we just don't use postmortems as punishment. If Jane deployed a bug, the postmortem doesn't say 'Jane is at fault' — it says 'the deploy process allowed the bug to reach production, the safeguards didn't catch it, the test coverage missed this case.' Jane may still need coaching privately; the postmortem focuses on systemic learning.

**Psychological safety is non-negotiable.** Engineers must feel safe admitting mistakes. If a postmortem says 'Jane did X' and Jane gets performance-managed, every future postmortem will hide details. Leadership must consistently protect blamelessness, even when tempting not to.

**5 Whys is a starting point, not a solution.** Toyota's 5-whys works for simple causal chains. Complex system failures have multiple contributing factors, not a single root cause. Use 5-whys to start, but expand to 'contributing factors' and systems thinking.

**Action items must be tracked to completion.** The number-one failure mode of postmortems is action items going into a doc and never getting done. Assign to tickets, track in a spreadsheet or system, nag weekly. No closure without completion.

**Publish widely.** Internal-only postmortems miss the multiplier effect. Teams in other services face similar problems and benefit from learning. Consider public postmortems for major incidents (GitHub, Cloudflare, AWS do this regularly and build trust).

**Meetings matter more than documents.** The postmortem meeting is where learning happens. Read the document together, ask questions, surface assumptions. Attendees should include responders, affected team, adjacent SREs, sometimes leadership.

**Don't conflate severity with postmortem worthiness.** Small near-miss incidents often teach more than big outages (less stress, clearer cause). Write postmortems for near-misses too.

**Quarterly trends analysis.** Look at postmortems across a quarter. What categories recur? Deploy-caused? DB-related? Third-party? Trends drive strategic investment (better deploy tooling, DB observability, vendor diversification).

**The action-items-done metric.** Track % action items completed on time. Below 70%? The system is broken — teams don't have bandwidth, or action items aren't prioritized, or ownership is fuzzy. Fix the process.

**Avoid 'we'll be more careful' action items.** Specific, actionable fixes: 'add pre-merge check for X', 'change alert threshold to Y', 'document runbook for Z'. Never 'be more careful' or 'improve reviews' — not actionable.

**Anonymize for external sharing.** Public postmortems from customer-facing services sometimes strip internal names while keeping the learning content. Legal may need to review.

**Integrate with on-call rotation.** On-call engineers should be trained on postmortem writing. First incident = paired postmortem with an experienced writer. Don't throw juniors into the deep end.

**Severity drives the depth.** SEV-1 (major outage, users affected): full template, group meeting, published. SEV-2 (degraded performance): shorter template, team review. SEV-3 (near-miss): brief writeup, 15-minute sync. Not every incident needs an hour-long group meeting.

**Use templates.** Don't reinvent the structure per incident. Template enforcement surfaces sections people skip. Google's SRE book has a template; many orgs publish theirs.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Six sections**: Summary, Timeline, Root cause & contributing factors, Resolution, What went well/poorly, Action items
- **Blameless means focus on systems**, not individuals; psychological safety makes honest reporting possible
- **Specific timeline** in UTC with minute-level granularity; vague times are useless
- **Multiple contributing factors**, not 'one root cause' — most real incidents have 3–5 factors
- **Action items must be SMART**: specific outcome, single owner, due date, linked ticket; avoid vague 'improve X'
- **Track to completion**: below 70% completion rate = broken process; nag weekly
- **Publish widely** — internal broadly, sometimes external; multiplies the learning effect
- **Postmortem meeting is where learning happens** — group read, questions, discussion; document is just the artifact
- **Quarterly trends analysis** drives strategic investment
- **Don't 'be more careful'** — always systemic fixes, never exhortations

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Every production incident costs the company — users affected, engineering time, revenue lost, trust dented. The postmortem is what the company receives in return — a written artifact that turns a painful incident into organizational learning.

**The key principle: blameless**
- Focus on systems, processes, and context that allowed the mistake — not on the individual
- An engineer who typed the wrong command was able to because the command wasn't behind safeguards, UI didn't warn, process didn't require review, training didn't cover it
- Fixing 'the engineer' doesn't prevent recurrence; fixing 'the system' does
- Blameless doesn't mean responsibility-free — engineers still own their work; we just don't use postmortems as punishment

**Why psychological safety matters**
- Engineers must feel safe admitting mistakes
- If a postmortem says 'Jane did X' and Jane gets performance-managed, every future postmortem hides details
- Leadership must protect blamelessness consistently, even when tempting not to

**The standard six-section template**

*Summary*
- Service, date, duration, severity, impact (users affected, revenue), root cause category, authors
- TL;DR that someone can read in 30 seconds

*Timeline*
- Minute-by-minute in UTC with specific timestamps
- '14:14 rollback attempted, blocked by stuck Argo sync' not 'about 10 minutes in we tried to rollback'
- Vague times are useless for analysis

*Root cause and contributing factors*
- Not 'Jane pushed a bug to production'
- Multiple factors: the bug passed tests because load tests used 10 RPS, production sees 500; canary deployed 100% too fast; auto-rollback wasn't configured; manual rollback was blocked by unrelated issue
- Most real incidents have 3-5 contributing factors; each is a potential action item

*Resolution*
- Short-term mitigation (scaled old version), long-term fix (query optimization)

*What went well, what went poorly*
- Both sides matter
- Went well: alert fired fast, runbook existed, team coordination was smooth
- Went poorly: canary ramp too aggressive, auto-rollback missing, load tests unrepresentative
- Celebrating what worked reinforces good behavior; examining what didn't reveals systemic gaps

*Action items — SMART*
- Specific outcome, single owner, due date, linked ticket
- Never 'improve monitoring' or 'be more careful' — not actionable
- Examples: 'Configure auto-rollback on payment-service, @sre-team, 2026-04-29, PAY-1234'

**The lifecycle after writing**
- Draft within 48 hours while memory is fresh
- Team review within 5 days
- Group postmortem meeting — where learning actually happens, read the doc together, ask questions
- Publish widely (internal, sometimes public for major incidents — GitHub, Cloudflare, AWS build trust this way)
- Track action items weekly until complete; below 70% completion = broken process

**Things that kill postmortems**
- Blame-heavy language; engineers hide details in future incidents
- Action items without owners and dates; nothing happens
- Private postmortems; other teams miss the learning
- 'We'll be more careful' exhortations; not actionable, won't prevent recurrence
- Only writing SEV-1 postmortems; small near-misses teach more, less stress, clearer cause

**Quarterly trends analysis**
- Look at postmortems across a quarter
- What categories recur: deploy-caused, DB-related, third-party, network?
- Trends drive strategic investment: better deploy tooling, DB observability, vendor diversification
- Without this, postmortems are local learning only; trends give org-wide insight

**The strategic answer**
- Postmortems are an investment; pay by writing, earn by preventing recurrence
- Culture makes it work: blamelessness, action-item discipline, meeting rigor
- Templates enforce structure so nothing gets skipped
- Publish widely; multiply the learning
- Track completion; unfinished action items are unfinished lessons
